organic_material.description: The amount of organic material present in grams per liter. This is a float type value.

salt_presence.description: Indicates whether salt is present (true) or not (false) in the water.

temperature.description: The water temperature in degrees Celsius. If unspecified, defaults to average sea temperature. This is a float type value.

message.content:
The ocean’s hue isn’t fixed—it shifts across a spectrum of blues, greens, and even browns, depending on several factors:

| Factor | Effect on Color |
|--------|----------------|
| **Depth** | Shallow waters scatter more light → turquoise/greenish‑blue. Deeper zones absorb longer wavelengths → deep navy or indigo. |
| **Clarity / Turbidity** | Clear water lets sunlight penetrate deeper → vivid azure. Suspended particles (silt, plankton) give muddier green or brown tones. |
| **Algae & Phytoplankton** | High chlorophyll concentrations tint the surface greenish‑yellow. Bloom events can turn entire stretches bright yellow or orange. |
| **Sun Angle & Time of Day** | Midday sun produces crisp cyan/azure. Early morning or late afternoon casts warm reds/oranges over calm seas. |
| **Weather Conditions** | Overcast skies diffuse light, making the sea appear darker gray-blue. Stormy conditions often reveal muddy, dark hues as waves stir up sediment. |
| **Geographic Location** | Tropical reefs show vibrant turquoise because of clear, shallow sand flats. Arctic ice fronts may look pale blue-white under low-angle winter light. |

So while “the sea” is commonly imagined as a brilliant blue, its true palette ranges widely—from emerald green near coral beds to charcoal depths beneath storm clouds—shaped by physics, biology, and atmospheric interplay.
